draft.title: Trail shoes for wide feet: what actually changes
draft.metaDescription: Which trail shoes suit wide feet, and what last width, drop and outsole change.
draft.intro: If your feet are wide, last width matters more than any other number on the box, and two of the three shoes here are built on a wider last. The Ridge Wide is the one to start with for technical trail; the Fell Wide is the one for boggy ground, where its gaiter attachment earns its keep.

sections.heading: What last width actually means
sections.body: Last width is the shape the shoe is built around, not how much the upper stretches. The Ridge Wide uses engineered mesh with TPU overlays, which holds a wide forefoot without the overlays cutting in; the standard version uses plain mesh on a narrower last and will feel tight across the ball of the foot however you lace it.

sections.heading: Weight, and what you give up for it
sections.body: The Ridge Wide is 290 g against the standard model's 265 g, and the Fell Wide is 310 g. That 45 g spread is the price of the wider platform and, in the Fell's case, the gaiter attachment. On a two-hour run it is not something most people notice; on a long day it is.

sections.heading: Which to pick
sections.body: Technical trail and wet rock: the Ridge Wide. Boggy ground where you will want gaiters: the Fell Wide. Hard-packed paths and a normal-width foot: the standard Ridge, which is lighter and cheaper to replace.
